extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political economy; policymakers and general readers interested in theories of distribution of wealth
extracted.subtask_description: Statement and exposition of the laws governing distribution of wealth — rent, wages, and interest — derived from the fundamental principle of human action and the margin of cultivation/production. The text explains causal relations, examples, and implications for social and economic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principle of human action
rubrics_metrics.description: Men seek to gratify their desires with the least exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as the central axiom from which the laws of rent, wages, and interest are derived; competition induced by this principle equalizes rewards for equal exertions and determines the margins at which labor and capital are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of rent (rent depends on the margin of cultivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: RENT depends on the margin of cultivation, rising as it falls and falling as it rises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rent equals the surplus of produce of superior land over that of the poorest land in use; competition prevents returns to labor and capital being greater than on the poorest land in use, thus fixing rent as a margin phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between wages and interest is determined by the average power of increase which attaches to capital from its use in reproductive modes. As rent arises, interest will fall as wages fall, or will be determined by the margin of cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest is a corollary of the law of rent; illustrated by hypothetical 'capital-only' production (fool's paradise) and island examples showing that as rent takes a larger share of produce the return to capital must diminish to near replacement. Also: interest and wages move together with changes in the margin of cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages depend upon the margin of production, or upon the produce which labor can obtain at the highest point of natural productiveness open to it without the payment of rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wages fixed by the produce labor could secure when applied to the best natural opportunities open without rent; if the margin of cultivation sinks or rises, wages fall or rise accordingly. This is derived from the principle that men will choose the highest natural productiveness available and competition equalizes returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages fixed by what laborers could make for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Under conditions of freedom, wages will be fixed by what the men could make if laboring for themselves; the employer can only pay what labor could earn otherwise, except to overcome particular inducements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wages deviate temporarily above or below this line, competitive tendencies restore them; thus employer and employee interests are balanced by the outside option of self-employment or alternate uses of labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal-productivity/margin-of-cultivation determinant of general wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The wages which an employer must pay will be measured by the lowest point of natural productiveness to which production extends (the margin of cultivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As production extends to poorer land (or other lower-productivity opportunities), the margin falls and general wages fall; conversely, opening superior natural opportunities raises the margin and wages. This applies from simple to complex societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors producing relative differences of wages between occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between wages in occupations arise from agreeableness/disagreeableness, ease or difficulty of learning, constancy/inconstancy of employment, trust required, and probability of success (Adam Smith's list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These causes operate through supply and demand for particular kinds of labor and explain relative differences; they do not, however, determine the general rate of wages across the whole economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between apparent and real differences in wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Some high wages are apparent (prize-like or compensatory for hardship/uncertainty), while real differences arise from the greater or less rarity of qualities (skill, ability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent high wages (e.g., intermittent occupations, lottery-like rewards) redistribute among many; real higher wages reflect genuinely higher productive contribution relative to common wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply and demand cannot determine the general rate of wages
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is said that the general rate of wages is determined by supply and demand, the words are meaningless because supply and demand are relative—supply of labor is demand for produce and vice versa—so in the whole community one must be co-extensive with the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply/demand changes can alter relative wages for particular labor types but cannot produce a permanent, general rise or fall in wages across the economy; the general rate is governed by the margin of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages ultimately tied to the lowest and widest stratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages in all strata must ultimately depend upon wages in the lowest and widest stratum—the primary occupations that procure wealth directly from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because occupations shade into each other and workers can shift, the general rate of wages is anchored by wages obtainable in occupations with the most uniform demand and greatest freedom to engage (the primary, natural-resource-based occupations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural (necessary) minimum of wages / natural wages
rubrics_metrics.description: This necessary minimum of wages (called 'natural wages' by Smith and Ricardo) is the point at which enough will be left as wages to secure the maintenance or reproduction of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The margin of production cannot fall below the level that secures labor's maintenance; natural wages are encompassed by the law of wages as the lower bound of the margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases of land/capital conditions and wage outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where land is free and labor unassisted by capital, the whole produce will go to labor as wages. Where land is free and labor assisted by capital, wages will consist of the whole produce less what induces storing up of labor as capital. Where land is subject to ownership and rent arises, wages will be fixed by what labor could secure from the highest natural opportunities open without payment of rent. Where natural opportunities are monopolized, wages may be forced by competition to the minimum at which laborers will consent to reproduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated cases show how property regimes and capital interact with the margin to determine the share of produce that goes to labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation and co-ordination of the laws of distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent, wages, and interest spring from a common center: the fundamental law that men seek to gratify their desires with the least exertion; accepting the law of rent implies the law of wages and interest as necessary deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the 'current statement' (laws presented separately) with the 'true statement' (all three depend on the margin of cultivation) and argues for their mutual consistency and derivation from a single principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of rent explains stagnant wages and interest under material progress
rubrics_metrics.description: If with an increase of production the laborer gets no more and the capitalist no more, it is a necessary inference that the land owner reaps the whole gain; the increase of rent explains why wages and interest do not increase with material progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three factors unite to production—labor, capital, and land—and three parties divide the produce. Material progress increases rent (land values), which necessarily occurs at the expense of the value of labor and capital's share; the net produce after rent determines wages and interest.
